title: Indian American Founders Raise $24 Million to Build AI Workforce for Lenders
excerpt: Kastle's Series A round, led by Insight Partners, will fund AI agents that work across banks' existing systems. Co-founders Rishi Choudhary and Nitish Poddar say the agents have already processed $1.8 billion in transactions.
body:
• Kastle, a San Francisco startup founded by Rishi Choudhary and Nitish Poddar, has raised $24 million in Series A funding led by Insight Partners, with continued backing from Y Combinator and Commerce Ventures and new participation from Fifth Wall.
  • The company builds specialized AI agents that operate directly across banks' existing legacy core systems, avoiding multi-year, high-risk infrastructure replacements.
  • Kastle says its agents have already processed more than $1.8 billion in transactions, starting with consumer lending, where fragmented systems create high volumes of repetitive operational work.
  • The funding will expand engineering, product, and go-to-market teams and accelerate deployments with financial institutions.

Kastle, an agentic AI platform built for consumer lenders, has raised $24 million in Series A funding led by Insight Partners, the company announced last week. The San Francisco startup, founded by Rishi Choudhary and Nitish Poddar, is developing what it calls an "AI workforce" for banks and financial institutions — software agents that work inside the legacy systems banks already run, rather than forcing them through wholesale technology replacements.

The round saw continued participation from Y Combinator and Commerce Ventures, with new investment from Fifth Wall and a group of founders and financial-services executives, according to Tech Startups' funding roundup. The announcement, reported widely on September 21, lands in a crowded field of AI agent startups — but Kastle is betting that deep workflow knowledge, not the most novel model, wins in regulated industries.

The adoption gap Kastle is targeting

Large banks recognize AI's potential but have been slow to deploy it, and Kastle's pitch is aimed squarely at the reason why. Replacing core banking infrastructure can require years of complex, high-risk migration, in a world where the underlying technology shifts every quarter. Layering conventional AI assistants on top of existing systems, meanwhile, captures only a fraction of AI's potential because assistants don't do the operational work itself.

"For years, enterprises have effectively been presented with a false choice: accept the limitations of legacy operations or endure a long and risky replacement of the systems at the heart of their business," said Rishi Choudhary, Kastle's co-founder and CEO. "Kastle creates a third path."

The company's platform deploys specialized agents that execute high-volume, routine workflows directly within banks' existing core systems: moving information between systems, reviewing documents, and executing defined processes. The agents keep systems of record updated and operate within existing processes and controls, a design meant to preserve oversight and regulatory compliance — the non-negotiable requirement for any bank deployment.

Starting with consumer lending

Kastle is beginning with consumer lending, where the operational complexity is among the highest in financial services. Lenders must process large volumes of time-sensitive work across fragmented systems while meeting stringent risk-management and regulatory standards. The company says its agents have already processed more than $1.8 billion in transactions while performing operational work for major enterprises and banks, with later reports putting the figure past $2 billion.

The platform is designed around hybrid operating teams: AI agents handle high-volume, repeatable work while human employees concentrate on cases requiring judgment, expertise, customer relationships, and empathy. It is a division of labor that financial institutions — with high labor costs, strong automation incentives, and little tolerance for uncontrolled model behavior — find easier to adopt than fully autonomous systems.

Why investors are betting on workflow depth

Insight Partners' involvement reflects a thesis gaining traction in enterprise AI: value accrues less to the company with the most novel model and more to the one that understands a regulated workflow deeply enough to execute it safely. In lending, integration depth, auditability, and process data can become stronger competitive barriers than access to a foundation model.

"Financial institutions do not need another layer of software that creates more work for their teams. They need AI that can reliably complete the work while ensuring compliance."

— Rebecca Liu-Doyle, Managing Director at Insight Partners

The $24 million will fund expansion of Kastle's engineering, product, and go-to-market teams, deepen the platform's capabilities, and accelerate deployments with financial institutions. For two Indian American founders, the raise continues a pattern of diaspora-led teams building enterprise AI companies at the intersection of technology and regulated industry — where execution on compliance matters as much as the technology itself.

What's next

Kastle's near-term test is converting pilot deployments into bank-wide rollouts — the graveyard of many enterprise AI promises. With capital from one of venture's most established growth firms and a product thesis tuned to banks' risk aversion, the company has a window to establish itself as the agentic layer for consumer lending before larger AI platforms turn their attention to the same workflows.
